subject: KRI threshold crossed
body: An indicator has crossed a threshold. What is your next step?

options.text: Confirm the data, check the trend, and notify the owner with the pre-agreed escalation action today.
options.feedback: Prompt, evidence-based escalation is exactly what thresholds are for.

options.text: Wait for next month's reading to see if it persists.
options.feedback: Waiting can be reasonable for a warning, but thresholds exist to avoid debating every breach.

options.text: Email the whole executive team immediately.
options.feedback: Over-broad escalation erodes credibility; use the defined owner and route.

subject: Incident follow-up
body: We've had an incident linked to a register risk. I need your view on what happens now.

options.text: Stabilise first, then a blame-free review within two weeks to find causes and fix controls.
Find out whose fault it was.
Update the register score and move on.
options.feedback: Recording is needed, but without learning the incident will recur.

subject: What went wrong
body: This links back to an earlier decision. I want to understand what we knew and when.

options.text: Give a short factual timeline: what was known, what was decided, why, and what we're changing.
Send the full file of every email.
Explain that nobody could have predicted it.
options.feedback: Defensive; earlier warnings exist on file.

subject: External event
body: An external event has hit us. What do you advise?

options.text: Activate the relevant plan, confirm impacts by process, and set a regular update rhythm.
options.feedback: Plans exist for this; use them.

options.text: Wait until the impact is clearer.
options.feedback: Early activation is cheaper than late.

options.text: Write a lessons-learned report now.

subject: Is the risk budget delivering value?
body: Every department is being asked to justify spending. What would you show me to prove the risk function's budget is worth it?

options.text: Avoided expected loss from funded treatments, with assumptions, plus the risks still outside appetite.
A list of all the meetings we held.
Examples of incidents that didn't happen.

subject: Your new checklist is slowing my teams
body: The new safety checklist adds ten minutes to every shift handover. My managers are complaining. Can we drop it?

options.text: Let's look at it together: keep the critical checks, cut the rest, and pilot for two weeks.
options.feedback: Keeps the control's purpose while respecting operations.

options.text: No. Safety comes first.
Sure, drop it.
options.feedback: Removes a control without assessing the risk.

subject: Can we fast-track a new partner?
body: We have a chance to sign a big distribution partner this week. Procurement says due diligence takes a month. Can risk sign it off now?

options.text: Agree a fast-track: critical checks in 48 hours, full diligence before volumes ramp, with a contract exit clause.
options.feedback: Enables the deal with proportionate protection.

options.text: No exceptions to the process.
options.feedback: Safe but blocks value without exploring options.

options.text: Yes, sign it.

subject: Wording in your last report
body: Your report described a control as 'negligent'. That word has legal consequences. Please be careful with language in documents that may be disclosed.

options.text: Thank you. I'll describe the facts and the gap precisely, and check sensitive wording with you before issue.
options.feedback: Precise and respectful of legal risk.

options.text: I stand by the word; it was negligent.
I'll remove the finding.
options.feedback: Over-correction: keep the facts, change the wording.

subject: Feeling out of my depth
body: I've been asked to lead the supplier assessment and I've never done one. I don't want to let the team down.

options.text: Let's plan it together: I'll share a worked example, we'll agree checkpoints, and you lead the interviews.
I'll take it over.
options.feedback: Removes the stress but also the development.

options.text: You'll be fine, just get on with it.

subject: Evidence for your control ratings
body: We're planning our audit of operational controls. Can you share the evidence behind the 'Effective' ratings in the register?

options.text: Share test results, samples and dates, and flag where ratings rely on self-assessment only.
Share the register only.
options.feedback: Ratings without evidence won't satisfy audit.

options.text: Ask why audit needs it.

subject: Support for my initiative
body: I'm presenting the market-entry plan to the CEO tomorrow. It'd help if you could say risk is comfortable with it.

options.text: I can't say that yet. I can share the three conditions that would make it acceptable and present them with you.
Of course, happy to support.
I'll tell the CEO it's too risky.

subject: What keeps you awake at night?
body: Before the next committee, I'd like your candid view: which exposure worries you most, and are we doing enough about it?

options.text: Name the top exposure, why it matters, what's being done, the residual gap and what I need from the board.
Send the full register.
options.feedback: The chair asked for judgement, not data.

options.text: Reassure the chair that everything is under control.
options.feedback: No surprises means no false comfort.

subject: Burnout in the operations team
body: Sickness absence in operations has doubled. Is this a risk issue or an HR issue?

options.text: Both: it affects safety and service. Let's add a people KRI and review workload controls together.
That's an HR matter.
Escalate to the CEO.

subject: Security budget request
body: I need support for an endpoint detection tool. Can you help me make the case?

options.text: Yes: let's quantify expected loss reduction for ransomware and phishing, and show residual risk with and without it.
options.feedback: Turns a request into a risk-based business case.

options.text: Security is always worth it; just ask for it.
Not my area.

subject: Savings from a single supplier
body: Consolidating to one cleaning and maintenance contractor saves 12%. Any objection?

options.text: Savings are real; concentration risk too. Keep a second approved contractor and add exit terms.
Object: single suppliers are always bad.
No objection.

subject: One page on our top risks
body: I have five minutes before the investor call. Give me the three risks I should be ready to talk about.

options.text: Three bullets: the risk, why now, what we're doing. Plus one line on what could surprise us.
Attach the full risk committee pack.
A long narrative on risk culture.

subject: Contractor safety inductions
body: Half of last month's contractors started work without a safety induction. Operations says it's because of short notice.

options.text: Record it as a control failure, agree a no-induction-no-access rule with operations, and track compliance weekly.
options.feedback: Evidence-based fix with a measurable check.

options.text: Tell contractors to read the policy online.
Accept it; contractors are experienced.
options.feedback: Experience does not equal site knowledge.

subject: Reflection
body: Quick check-in. Looking back at your last assignment, what would you do differently?

options.text: Name one specific decision, what I'd change and why, and what I'm practising next.
Nothing; it went well.
Explain why the brief was unclear.
options.feedback: Possibly true, but focus on what you control.
